definition: A billionaire whose wealth and political power materially reinforce one another through preferential access, policy influence, state patronage, or a documented exchange securing private economic advantage.
method: Case-based editorial assessment, not a numerical corruption score. Historical and disputed evidence is labeled. Wealth, nationality, inheritance, office, monopoly, donations, contracts or sanctions alone do not determine a verdict.
limitations: Initial research, AI-assisted and not independently editorially reviewed. Coverage is uneven and mostly unassessed. Historical evidence does not establish ongoing 2026 conduct. Narrow source checks must not be treated as exoneration.

alisher-usmanov.period: Historical relationships; official records checked in 2026
alisher-usmanov.summary: Likely under our definition: official accounts describe political relationships that both sustain power and benefit his business interests.

support.text: US Treasury attributes enrichment to Kremlin ties and alleges financial links to Putin and benefits provided to Medvedev. These are government assertions, not criminal findings.
The UK statement identifies financial or material benefit from Putin, beyond simply operating in a strategic sector.

counter.text: German prosecutors agreed to end a sanctions probe after a €10m payment, without an admission of guilt. A separate money-laundering investigation had been dropped in 2024. Neither should be presented as a conviction.

alisher-usmanov.limitations: The inference relies on sanctioning authorities’ accounts. Their designation standards differ from proof of corruption, and this is not a criminal verdict.
alisher-usmanov.reviewDepth: Initial source-led assessment; not independently reviewed

mikhail-gutseriev.summary: Likely: the cited records describe business-backed support for an entrenched ruler and economic benefits from that government.
mikhail-gutseriev.mechanism: Regime support ↔ access to strategic business

support.text: The UK describes a longstanding Lukashenko associate providing support through his business interests.
The reasons include economic benefit or support, business control in energy and extractives, and association with Lukashenko.

counter.text: The designation is an administrative measure with alternative grounds, not a court finding of a specific corrupt bargain. Strategic-sector investment alone would not meet our test.

mikhail-gutseriev.limitations: Independent transaction-level corroboration and a detailed response from the subject remain research gaps. Moderate, not high, confidence.
mikhail-gutseriev.reviewDepth: Initial source-led assessment; not independently reviewed

jay-y-lee.period: 2015 merger / prior bribery case; subsequent pardon and acquittal
jay-y-lee.summary: Likely on the historical record: a separate bribery conviction establishes an attempted exchange of money for state support of family business control.

support.text: Lee was convicted of bribing President Park and her confidante for government support of the merger that strengthened his control of Samsung.

counter.text: He was pardoned in 2022. In July 2025, the Supreme Court finally upheld his acquittal in the separate merger financial-crimes case. This assessment does not allege ongoing bribery.

jay-y-lee.limitations: Historical mechanism, not a claim that every act of the merger was criminal or that the conduct continues in 2026. Other Samsung family members do not inherit this assessment.
jay-y-lee.reviewDepth: Initial source-led assessment; not independently reviewed

prajogo-pangestu.period: Soeharto-era wealth formation; not a 2026 conduct finding
prajogo-pangestu.summary: Likely on the historical record: World Bank research places him among the beneficiaries of politically allocated timber concessions and privileged finance.
prajogo-pangestu.mechanism: Political loyalty ↔ concessions and subsidized finance

support.text: The report’s state-capture case study names Prayogo Pangestu among Soeharto associates dominating timber concessions, describing discretionary rights and directed concessional state-bank loans.
support.source: World Bank, Combating Corruption in Indonesia, printed p.69 / PDF p.106

counter.text: This account concerns the New Order forestry system. It does not establish current political control or wrongdoing in today’s energy businesses.

prajogo-pangestu.limitations: The historical political allocation is stronger evidence than nationality or company size; a present-day feedback relationship still needs research.
prajogo-pangestu.reviewDepth: Initial source-led assessment; not independently reviewed

vladimir-potanin.summary: Likely on the historical record: he helped shape the privatization mechanism from which his business obtained a major state asset.

support.text: Treisman traces the loans-for-shares proposal to Potanin, his acquisition of a Norilsk Nickel stake, and his later deputy-premier role. The paper documents auction restrictions and apparent cronyism.
support.source: Daniel Treisman, NBER working paper 15819, pp.10–12,23

counter.text: The same paper challenges exaggerated underpricing claims and finds subsequent operating improvements; it also describes limits on oligarchs’ political power. This is not evidence that Potanin controlled the government.

vladimir-potanin.limitations: A historical editorial inference, not a finding about every subsequent asset or a verified description of his 2026 influence.
vladimir-potanin.reviewDepth: Initial source-led assessment; not independently reviewed

roman-abramovich.summary: Likely under our definition, based on the UK’s specific account of political access yielding business concessions—not merely his sanctions status.

support.text: The 2022 UK statement alleged tax concessions, favorable state share transactions and pre-World-Cup contracts linked to preferential treatment by Putin.
support.source: UK notice archived by Bermuda Monetary Authority, RUS0270

counter.text: The General Court rejected his latest sanctions challenge in September 2026, applying business/sector criteria. That decision is not a criminal conviction or independent proof of each alleged favor; a legal appeal remained possible.

roman-abramovich.limitations: The specific patronage narrative is an authority’s attribution, disputed through legal challenges. Current screening reasons are not identical to the historical 2022 statement.
roman-abramovich.reviewDepth: Initial source-led assessment; not independently reviewed

mikhail-fridman.summary: Mixed / disputed: proximity and sector exposure are documented, but a court found the evidence insufficient for important earlier support-or-benefit allegations.

support.text: The UK designation cites Alfa-related financial-sector business. This establishes the authority’s designation rationale, not personal control of public policy.

counter.text: The General Court annulled listings covering February 2022–March 2023: proximity alone did not sufficiently establish support for, or benefit from, Russian decision-makers. This did not annul every later sanction.

mikhail-fridman.limitations: Neither “sanctioned therefore oligarch” nor “all sanctions cleared” is a defensible reading. Further individual evidence is needed.
mikhail-fridman.reviewDepth: Initial source-led assessment; not independently reviewed

elon-musk.period: 2025 government role and disputed Starlink benefit
elon-musk.summary: Mixed / disputed: unusual public power and private business interests overlap, with a specific allegation of trade leverage benefiting Starlink. That alleged exchange is not established here as a finding.
elon-musk.mechanism: Public office / trade leverage → alleged private benefit

support.text: Democratic senators requested an investigation into reports of US trade diplomacy helping Starlink gain foreign approvals. This is a partisan oversight allegation, not an investigation’s conclusion.

counter.text: AP reported his departure from the temporary government role in May 2025. A historical appointment is not current office or proof of a corrupt exchange.
The lunar-lander procurement documents a major contract, not favoritism. Ordinary government purchasing does not independently meet our definition.

elon-musk.limitations: No adjudicated finding of the alleged Starlink exchange is established by the reviewed sources. These records do not comprehensively assess all political activity.
elon-musk.reviewDepth: Initial source-led assessment; not independently reviewed

gautam-adani-1.reviewDepth: Primary-source-led episode review (wave 37); not independently editorially reviewed; not exoneration
gautam-adani-1.confidence: Moderate / legal status well documented; underlying allegation never adjudicated
gautam-adani-1.period: Alleged conduct 2020–2024; US charges and SEC complaint 20 Nov 2024; SEC consent 14 May 2026; DOJ dismissal motion 18 May 2026; court order Aug 2026; SEBI orders Sept 2025 and Sept 2026
gautam-adani-1.summary: Gautam Adani is the subject of three separate legal tracks that must not be merged. (1) The alleged 2020–2024 Indian power-contract bribery scheme: the SEC alleged that he and Sagar Adani orchestrated promises of hundreds of millions of dollars in bribes and misled US bond investors; in May 2026 both consented to SEC judgments without admitting or denying (USD 6 million and USD 12 million penalties). In the criminal case, a federal judge in August 2026 dismissed with prejudice the three counts charged against Gautam Adani (securities-fraud conspiracy, wire-fraud conspiracy, securities fraud) on the Justice Department’s motion, expressly taking no view of the merits and calling the process irregular; the FCPA and obstruction counts, charged only against other, non-appearing defendants, remained undecided at the last reviewed order. No court has found that bribes were paid. (2) The Hindenburg allegations: SEBI’s September 2025 final order found them not established; its September 2026 order found minimum-public-shareholding and fraud allegations not established against twelve noticees (including Vinod Adani) while the group companies and Gautam Adani settled separately without admission. (3) A separate USD 275 million OFAC sanctions settlement by Adani Enterprises, unrelated to the bribery allegation.
gautam-adani-1.mechanism: Alleged payments to Indian state officials → above-market power-purchase commitments (unadjudicated); separately, documented 2026 US process questions about dismissal

support.text: The SEC alleged that Gautam Adani and Sagar Adani orchestrated a scheme to pay or promise hundreds of millions of dollars in bribes to Indian officials in exchange for commitments to buy energy at above-market rates benefiting Adani Green, and falsely touted anti-bribery compliance in a September 2021 bond offering. Each consented to judgment, subject to court approval, without admitting or denying; penalties USD 6 million (Gautam) and USD 12 million (Sagar). Case 1:24-cv-08080 (EDNY).
support.kind: Regulator allegation and no-admission consent settlement

support.text: Garaufis’s order summarizes the October 2024 indictment: it alleged about USD 265 million in bribes for solar contracts, a financing-fraud scheme and an obstruction scheme. Count One (FCPA conspiracy) was charged only against non-appearing defendants; Gautam Adani, Sagar Adani and Vneet Jaain were charged in Counts Two to Four (securities-fraud conspiracy, wire-fraud conspiracy, securities fraud). These are charging-document allegations recited by the court, not findings. The order also records that Adani Green is India-based and that the SEC complaints allege bribes to Indian state officials.
support.kind: Court recital of charges (allegation, not finding)
support.access: Full 47-page text extracted and read; the order’s printed date is illegible in the text layer, 10 August 2026 is per the SEC notice and press reports

support.text: The same order records that counsel for Adani presented about 600 pages to DOJ, that Principal Associate Deputy AG R. Trent McCotter says he was the sole decision-maker and worked with defense counsel, and that defense counsel twice told DOJ a USD 10 billion US investment could be part of a resolution. The EDNY US Attorney wrote that this proposal was categorically rejected by his office; McCotter says it played no role; Adani swore he knew of no agreement. The judge called the irregularities concerning but stated that the ruling expresses no opinion on the merits.
support.source: US v. Adani, Memorandum & Order, sections I.D–I.F and Conclusion
support.kind: Court record of process (documented, not adjudicated as an exchange)

support.text: DOJ’s one-paragraph Rule 48(a) motion asked to dismiss the whole indictment with prejudice, citing prosecutorial discretion “not to devote further resources” to charges against individuals; counsel for all defendants consented; signed by McCotter and US Attorney Joseph Nocella Jr.
support.access: Full 2-page filing and proposed order text read

support.text: On 8 July 2026 the court noted McCotter’s letter raised, for the first time, the possibility of an unmemorialized agreement tied to the dismissal and ordered Gautam Adani to answer by sworn affidavit whether anything was promised, offered or agreed in connection with the dismissal.

OFAC announced a USD 275 million settlement with Adani Enterprises Limited for 32 apparent Iran-sanctions violations (LPG purchases, about USD 192 million in payments, November 2023–June 2025), found egregious and not voluntarily self-disclosed. This is a corporate sanctions matter, not evidence for the bribery or political-exchange mechanism; it is excluded from the rubric.
support.source: US Treasury OFAC recent actions, 18 May 2026
support.access: Notice page read; the linked enforcement release PDF was not opened

counter.text: Reuters reports Judge Garaufis dismissed the criminal case on 10 August 2026 at prosecutors’ request, said he was satisfied the USD 10 billion pledge did not factor into the decision, and criticized the process. Adani: “I welcome the U.S. Court’s decision with humility and deep respect for the judicial process.” The Adani Group denies wrongdoing.
counter.kind: Subject response and material case update
counter.access: Syndicated summary read; full Reuters text not available

counter.text: The court granted the motion only in part: Counts Two to Four against Gautam Adani, Sagar Adani and Jaain were dismissed with prejudice; judgment was reserved on Counts One and Five against five non-appearing defendants pending DOJ reasons by 31 August 2026. Footnote 44: no one should take the ruling as agreement with DOJ’s decision or an opinion on the merits. No later filing was found in this review.
counter.source: US v. Adani, Memorandum & Order: disposition
counter.kind: Legal status (not a finding of innocence or guilt)

counter.text: The SEC’s covered-action notice lists SEC v. Gautam Adani and Sagar Adani (24-cv-08080) with a qualifying judgment/order date of 10 August 2026; the May release stated the consents were subject to court approval. The notice does not state the type of judgment, so entry of the consent judgments is inferred, not confirmed.

The Adani Group called the DOJ and SEC allegations against Adani Green directors baseless and denied, noted the charges are unproven and defendants presumed innocent, and said it would pursue all legal remedies.
counter.source: b360 Nepal report of the Adani Group statement
counter.access: Short secondary report read; the original statement was not located

counter.text: SEBI’s final order (Kamlesh C. Varshney, whole-time member) found the Hindenburg-linked allegations about transactions with Milestone Tradelinks and Rehvar Infrastructure not established against Adani Ports, Adani Power, Adani Enterprises, Gautam Adani and others: the entities were not related parties under rules then in force, there was no allegation of siphoning, and the money had come back with interest before the investigation. Proceedings disposed of without direction.

The Supreme Court refused to transfer the Hindenburg-related investigation to an SIT or the CBI, found no regulatory failure attributable to SEBI, said third-party reports could not be conclusive proof of inadequate investigation, and directed SEBI and agencies to probe whether Hindenburg’s and others’ short positions involved any infraction. It did not adjudicate the Adani bribery allegations, which arose later.
counter.source: Vishal Tiwari v. Union of India, 2024 INSC 3 (SEBI-hosted copy)

counter.text: SEBI’s 28 September 2026 final order found the minimum-public-shareholding and PFUTP fraud allegations not established against Noticees 1–12 (including Vinod Adani and offshore investors) and penalised two of them for failing to furnish information. Noticees 13–30, including the four listed companies and Gautam Adani, had settled under SEBI’s settlement regulations by separate order, so this finding does not decide their case.
counter.access: Full 81-page order read; the separate settlement order was not opened

counter.text: PTI reports Gautam Adani, four group companies and others settled the MPS case for Rs 1.48 crore without admitting or denying; a week earlier five group companies settled a related-party-disclosure adjudication for about Rs 1.5 crore. Settlements are not findings of guilt or innocence.
counter.source: PTI via The New Indian Express
counter.access: Article text read; the underlying settlement orders were not opened

counter.text: Hindenburg’s January 2023 report alleged stock manipulation, offshore shell networks and accounting issues, and disclosed a short position. It alleged market conduct, not bribery of officials; it is context for the SEBI outcomes above, not support for the political-exchange mechanism.
counter.access: First 100,000 characters of the page read; the later part was not read

gautam-adani-1.limitations: Scope: only the alleged Indian power-contract bribery mechanism and the 2026 US dismissal process are scored. Gautam Adani personally was not charged in the FCPA count; the SEC complaint does attribute orchestration to him. The criminal case is not fully closed on the record read (Counts One and Five, other defendants) and no filing after 12 August 2026 was found. A consent judgment’s entry is inferred, not confirmed. No Indian criminal proceeding, CAG report, Parliament answer or the alleged political relationships with Indian governments were reviewed; Sagar Adani, Vinod Adani and Adani companies are separate persons. Neither the dismissal nor the settlements nor the SEBI findings determine the wider political-economy question, and the allegation is not a finding of bribery.

rupert-murdoch.period: UK press / political relationships assessed in 2017
rupert-murdoch.summary: Mixed / disputed: political agenda-setting power is documented, but a specific exchange securing business favors is not established by the reviewed regulator’s account.
rupert-murdoch.mechanism: Media power → political access; return benefit unresolved

support.text: Ofcom discusses the Murdoch family’s access to senior politicians and influence over the political agenda.

counter.text: Ofcom cautions that frequent meetings do not themselves prove influence over decisions, and that the degree of influence is difficult to evidence.

rupert-murdoch.limitations: This historical UK review is not a current global account of the family’s media control. Media ownership alone is insufficient.
rupert-murdoch.reviewDepth: Initial source-led assessment; not independently reviewed

jeff-bezos.summary: Mixed / disputed: overlapping media ownership and government-facing business create a plausible conflict, but the claimed exchange is not established.
jeff-bezos.mechanism: Media decisions ↔ government-facing business: disputed link

support.text: AP reported the Washington Post’s non-endorsement decision alongside a meeting between Blue Origin executives and Trump. Timing raises a question, not proof of a bargain.

counter.text: Bezos denied that the non-endorsement involved a quid pro quo and said he had not known of the Blue Origin meeting beforehand.

jeff-bezos.limitations: Low confidence: temporal coincidence, media ownership and public contracts cannot establish oligarchy on their own.
jeff-bezos.reviewDepth: Initial source-led assessment; not independently reviewed

michael-bloomberg.reviewDepth: Source-led review of the stated episode; not independently reviewed
michael-bloomberg.period: Mayoral and presidential-campaign relationships discussed in 2020
michael-bloomberg.summary: His wealth clearly financed political reach. The reviewed analysis links philanthropy to political support, but shows less about political power generating private commercial returns.
michael-bloomberg.mechanism: Personal wealth and philanthropy → political influence; commercial return unresolved

support.text: Brookings scholar Vanessa Williamson argued that Bloomberg’s philanthropic funding gave leverage over institutions and potential political supporters. This is attributed political analysis, not an adjudicated finding that grants bought endorsements.

counter.text: Bloomberg ended his presidential campaign after failing to secure a path to nomination despite extensive spending. Wealth did not guarantee electoral control.

michael-bloomberg.limitations: This assessment does not equate charitable giving or running for office with corruption. It is limited to political influence discussed in the reviewed record, not a full examination of Bloomberg LP contracts.

larry-page.reviewDepth: Narrow source-led review under a limited search budget; not independently editorially reviewed; no rubric assigned
larry-page.summary: Page co-founded Google. The reviewed pages describe company-level antitrust litigation (US v. Google) and, per a Wikipedia summary of a 2026 press report, Page and Brin moving or closing 60 California LLCs in December 2025 around a proposed state billionaire tax. None of the pages read names Page personally in a political donation, appointment, or state benefit.

Google on 2 September 2025, barring exclusive contracts for Google Search, Chrome, Assistant and Gemini and requiring some index and interaction data sharing with rivals. The August 2024 opinion found Google maintained a monopoly in general search. This is a company case; Page is not mentioned in the release.
support.source: US Department of Justice press release

support.text: Summary of the case: liability ruling 5 August 2024 (Judge Mehta), remedies September 2025 with no Chrome/Android divestiture, supplementary December 2025 order, appeals pending as of early 2026. The page does not name Page or Brin.
support.source: Wikipedia: United States v. Google LLC (2020)
support.access: Page text reviewed; tertiary source via fetch tool, cited links not verified

support.text: Role-only: article reports that in December 2025 Brin and Page (combined $520 billion per the page) moved or closed 60 California LLCs, which the article ties to the 2026 billionaire-tax initiative. Motive is the article's inference, not an adjudicated finding; Page-specific conduct is not separately detailed in the text read.
support.access: Page text reviewed; tertiary source via fetch tool, cited links not verified

counter.text: The antitrust case is against the company and its outcome was a conduct remedy, not a state benefit to the founder. Restructuring assets in response to a tax proposal is lawful planning absent further facts, and no benefit linked to public power was found.
counter.access: Page text reviewed; tertiary source via fetch tool, cited links not verified

larry-page.limitations: Not read: FEC, OpenSecrets or LDA records for Alphabet and Page personally; the NYT original; Alphabet proxy statements. Rubric dimensions (leverage, benefit, exchange) lack receipts specific to Page. A narrow review, not exoneration.

mark-zuckerberg.reviewDepth: Source-led review of the stated episode; not independently reviewed
mark-zuckerberg.summary: Corporate political access and regulatory interests overlap. The reviewed records support a possible influence channel, not a demonstrated bargain that bought regulatory protection.
mark-zuckerberg.mechanism: Political giving and access → sought regulatory influence; payoff unproven

support.text: Senators Warren and Bennet questioned Meta’s inaugural donation and its regulatory interests. Their letter raises an influence concern; it is not an adjudicated finding of purchased favors.
support.source: US Senate: letter to Zuckerberg, pages 10–12

mark-zuckerberg.limitations: The Senate letter is a political inquiry, not a neutral finding. Do not transfer a corporate donation into personal bribery or treat a favorable court ruling as proof of influence. This episode is not a comprehensive global assessment.

larry-ellison.reviewDepth: Source-led review of the stated episode; not independently reviewed
larry-ellison.summary: High-level access and the regulatory conditions on an Ellison-family investment create a concrete political-economic intersection. The record does not establish that Larry personally made an improper bargain.
larry-ellison.mechanism: Family-backed media acquisition ↔ political regulatory conditions

The FCC order identifies Larry and David as the Ellison family investors, while specifying David’s managerial and voting control.
support.access: Official indexed passage reviewed; direct retrieval unavailable

support.text: Reuters reported merger clearance following commitments on newsroom oversight and diversity policy. These are concrete regulatory conditions affecting the family investment.

counter.text: The FCC record assigns operational control to David. Larry’s backing and political access are not proof that he personally negotiated each condition or committed a crime.
counter.access: Official indexed passage reviewed; direct retrieval unavailable

mukesh-ambani.reviewDepth: Deep source-led review of dated episodes; primary documents read where retrievable; not independently editorially reviewed; not exoneration where no estimate is given
mukesh-ambani.period: 2010–2013 (BWA auction and unified licence); 2014–2026 (KG-D6); 2018 (Jio Institute); 2023–2026 (satellite spectrum policy)
mukesh-ambani.summary: Reviewed on separate dated episodes. (1) 2010–13 BWA spectrum and unified licence: a 2015 CAG report put the undue benefit to Jio at Rs 3,367 crore (a 2014 draft said Rs 22,842 crore); the Supreme Court in April 2016 held the migration policy “valid, legal and without any blemish” and found no undue favour. (2) KG-D6: a 2014 FIR is an allegation whose outcome I could not verify; the later cost and gas-migration disputes are arbitration and court proceedings in which the government has won and lost. (3) 2018 Jio Institute: an official selection panel chose it in a greenfield category over a reported internal Finance Ministry objection. (4) 2023–26 satellite spectrum: Jio’s filed position is auction-only, yet the Telecommunications Act 2023 and TRAI’s 2025 recommendations point to administrative assignment, the opposite outcome; Jio also has its own satellite plans and a 2025 SpaceX distribution agreement. In October 2026 Elon Musk’s unnamed-oligarch post was followed by a post asking whether Ambani is “the real boss of India”; the government called any discrimination claim baseless. None of these is an adjudicated exchange. No estimate is given.
mukesh-ambani.mechanism: Contested licensing and policy outcomes in telecom and energy; documented corporate lobbying positions; one audit finding, one judicial rejection, one unresolved allegation; no adjudicated exchange of favours

support.text: The Caravan, citing the final CAG report tabled on 8 May 2015, reports that the CAG found DoT gave Jio an “undue benefit” of Rs 3,367 crore by letting it offer voice on its 2010 BWA spectrum for a Rs 1,658 crore migration fee fixed in 2001. A draft CAG report of August 2014 had put the figure at Rs 22,842 crore. The CAG report itself was not retrieved; this is a detailed secondary account that also quotes its text.
support.kind: Audit finding as reported (CAG report itself not read)
support.access: Page text reviewed; secondary account of the CAG report

support.text: The Delhi government’s anti-corruption branch FIR, ordered in February 2014 after a complaint by four prominent citizens, alleged that the then oil minister, a former minister and others colluded with Ambani to raise gas prices. The Delhi High Court restrained coercive action but let investigation continue. These are allegations; the later outcome of the FIR was not found.
support.kind: Allegation by a state government; court order limiting coercive action
support.access: Page text reviewed (Business Today, Outlook 2015, DNA April 2015); article date approximate

support.text: PIB’s official 9 July 2018 release lists Jio Institute (Reliance Foundation) under the Green Field Category among six Institutions of Eminence out of 114 applications, 40 from private institutions. Indian Express RTI records, reported by Business Today, show the Finance Ministry’s expenditure department called the status for not-yet-established private institutions “beyond rationale and is not supported”; the tag was still granted.
support.source: PIB; Business Today (citing Indian Express RTI)
support.kind: Official selection plus internal-record report of a procedural objection
support.access: Page text reviewed (PIB 1538188 and Business Today)

support.text: In its 13 May 2026 filing to TRAI, Reliance Jio Infocomm states that “only legally tenable and technically suitable mode of spectrum assignment for satellite and NTN based communication services are through spectrum auction”, invokes “Same Service, Same Rules”, and urges that a foreign NGSO operator’s spectrum assignment be tied to reciprocal coordination rights for an Indian constellation. This documents a corporate policy position aligned with Jio’s disclosed plan for its own constellation; it is not evidence of how the government decided.
support.source: Reliance Jio Infocomm Ltd: comments to TRAI

support.text: MediaNama reports that after Musk’s 7 October 2026 post about “certain oligarchs” he asked in a follow-up “Is Ambani the real boss of India?”. The Next Web likewise reports the follow-up. This is an allegation by a commercial rival; the posts reviewed offer no supporting evidence, and the first post names no one.
support.kind: Allegation by commercial rival; no evidence presented
support.access: Page text reviewed; the X posts themselves were not opened

counter.text: In Centre for Public Interest Litigation v. Union of India (W.P.(C) 382/2014, bench of T.S. Thakur, A.K. Sikri, R. Banumathi), the Supreme Court dismissed the challenge to Jio’s voice permission. It held all BWA holders became eligible to migrate, so “it cannot be treated as a case of back door entry”; that Jio paid Rs 12,847.77 crore for spectrum plus Rs 1,658 crore, so a wrongful loss “cannot be said”; and that the CAG draft was not the final report, which “is materially different”.

counter.access: Judgment text (55 pp) searched and passages read via a third-party host; Business Today summary read

counter.text: A 2015 Solicitor-General opinion to DoT, reported by Voice&Data, rejected the CAG draft’s analysis as taking “a very narrow perspective”, noting auction rules allowed shareholding change after the auction. This is a law officer’s view, not an adjudication.

Reliance’s own 4 March 2025 exchange filing says the 2018 KG-D6 arbitration award rejecting the government’s roughly US$1.55 billion gas-migration claim was upheld by a single judge on 9 May 2023, then reversed by a Delhi High Court division bench on 14 February 2025; the petroleum ministry then demanded US$2.81 billion. RIL’s 2025-26 annual report says it filed a special leave petition on 14 May 2025 and the matter was listed for directions. The state has therefore not uniformly favoured Reliance in this dispute; RIL says it expects no liability.
counter.source: Reliance Industries stock-exchange filing; RIL Integrated Annual Report 2025-26 (note 34.4)
counter.kind: Primary corporate disclosure of adverse and pending litigation

counter.text: The HRD Ministry and the committee chair said Jio was one of 11 greenfield applicants and the only one to satisfy four stated criteria (land, qualified core team, funding, strategic plan), that only a letter of intent was issued with three years to qualify, and that private institutions get no government grant. The 2018 selection committee picked only 6 of 114 applicants. tadashi-yanai.limitations: No numerical estimate: policy advocacy is observable, but implemented influence and reciprocal economic benefit are not established here. This is not a full review of Fast Retailing’s government relations or international supply chain.

iris-fontbona.reviewDepth: Source-led review of stated episodes; broader coverage still limited
iris-fontbona.period: Chilean business-group research covering 2010–2020, published 2023; ownership profile, January 2024
iris-fontbona.summary: Research documents political resources around the Luksic business group. Fontbona’s ownership role matters, but group-level evidence does not yet isolate her personal direction of political activity or a reciprocal benefit.
iris-fontbona.mechanism: Controlling family wealth, revolving-door networks and media interests; individual attribution unresolved

support.source: Atenea: Oligarquía, poder material y recursos de poder en Chile, 2010–2020

The study distinguishes the Luksic group’s earlier commercial origins from its later participation in privatizations. It does not describe every part of the fortune as originating in privatization.

The Forbes “& family” label is a wealth attribution, not permission to assign every relative’s political conduct to the named person. Group-level scholarly classification is retained, not presented as an individual criminal finding.

zhong-shanshan.reviewDepth: Source-led review of stated episodes; broader coverage still limited
zhong-shanshan.period: Wuyishan agreement, 2017; park controversy, 2020; public backlash, March 2024
zhong-shanshan.summary: Nongfu Spring’s water project involved local-government cooperation and environmental controversy. That warrants scrutiny of allocation and oversight, but the reviewed material does not establish Zhong personally receiving political favors.

alexey-mordashov.reviewDepth: Source-led review of stated episodes; broader coverage still limited
alexey-mordashov.period: EU designation, February 2022; General Court judgment, September 2023
alexey-mordashov.summary: The EU attributed political-benefit and regime-support links to Mordashov’s holdings, and his 2023 sanctions challenge failed. Those records are substantial evidence to examine, but different legal grounds must not be collapsed into a proven personal patronage bargain.
alexey-mordashov.mechanism: Banking, media and industrial holdings ↔ attributed state support and benefit

support.text: The 2022 EU statement attributes benefit from political links and describes Severgroup’s connections to Bank Rossiya, National Media Group and Power Machines. These are the Council’s stated reasons, not a criminal conviction.

The General Court dismissed Mordashov’s challenge. Its summary includes the criterion covering leading businesspeople in revenue-generating sectors; that criterion is not itself a finding of a personal favor.

alexey-mordashov.limitations: No numerical estimate from this legal-record review alone. The underlying benefit mechanism and person-level political leverage need independent corroboration. This file describes historical reasons and a specific judgment, not an assertion about all current holdings, current sanctions in every jurisdiction, or criminal guilt.

klaus-michael-kuehne.reviewDepth: Source-led review of stated episodes; broader coverage still limited
klaus-michael-kuehne.period: HHLA privatization debate, September 2023–November 2024; separate opera agreement, 2025
klaus-michael-kuehne.summary: Kuehne publicly sought a city privatization arrangement favoring his holding company or Hapag-Lloyd. Hamburg instead completed its partnership with MSC. The estimate covers this unsuccessful commercial-policy effort, not his whole career.
klaus-michael-kuehne.mechanism: Personal advocacy for port ownership → requested city deal, not an achieved award

support.text: Reuters quotes Kuehne seeking an agreement with Hamburg to privatize HHLA toward his holding company or Hapag-Lloyd, in which he held a substantial stake. This identifies a personal request and a direct economic interest.

support.text: MSC subsequently announced completion of its HHLA joint venture with Hamburg, with the city retaining 50.1% and MSC holding 49.9%. Kuehne was not the successful private partner in this transaction.

Hamburg separately describes a foundation-led opera project with public participation and a capped €147.5 million city contribution for site-specific costs. This is a different agreement, not a reward from the port deal.
support.source: City of Hamburg: opera agreement summary

counter.text: Hamburg’s opera summary provides for the foundation’s shares to be donated to the city after completion and assigns additional construction risks to the foundation. Public spending on that project is not a personal cash grant to Kuehne.
counter.source: City of Hamburg: ownership and risk terms

klaus-michael-kuehne.limitations: The zero benefit component means the requested HHLA award did not go to him in this episode. It does not mean no benefit from any government anywhere. No causal exchange between opera philanthropy and shipping policy is established; the two projects are kept separate.

gianluigi-aponte.reviewDepth: Source-led review of stated episodes; broader coverage still limited
gianluigi-aponte.period: Genoa terminal-concession contacts in 2021, reported June 2024; ownership update announced April 2026
gianluigi-aponte.summary: Reporting on the Genoa port case describes Aponte personally contacting political leadership about a concession connected to his business interests. This supports a specific access–benefit relationship, while the reporting expressly identifies him as a witness, not a suspect.
gianluigi-aponte.mechanism: Personal mayoral access ↔ long-term port-concession interest

support.access: Indexed article passages reviewed; direct retrieval failed

counter.text: Rai reports that Aponte was heard as a witness and was not under investigation in this proceeding at the time. An alleged payment by another businessman must not be attributed to him.

Reuters reports MSC’s April 2026 announcement that ownership had passed to Diego and Alexa in late 2025, while Gianluigi remained executive chairman. Historical ownership and present executive influence are not interchangeable.

gianluigi-aponte.limitations: Historical, episode-limited estimate. The underlying intercept and concession contract were not independently inspected. A report of access is not proof of an unlawful personal bargain, and being a witness is not an accusation. The fixed Forbes annual wealth snapshot is retained rather than silently rewritten after the ownership announcement.

rafaela-aponte-diamant.reviewDepth: Source-led review of stated episodes; broader coverage still limited
rafaela-aponte-diamant.period: MSC Foundation governance reviewed October 2026; UK subsidiary control filing effective February 2026
rafaela-aponte-diamant.summary: Rafaela’s foundation governance and historical company-control role are documented separately from her husband’s political contacts. The reviewed records do not establish that she directed those contacts or secured a preferential public decision.
rafaela-aponte-diamant.mechanism: Foundation governance and historical corporate control; personal political mechanism unresolved

rafaela-aponte-diamant.limitations: No numerical estimate: do not copy Gianluigi’s contacts, scores or allegations onto Rafaela. A control filing is not evidence of misconduct, and its effective date does not authorize replacing the Forbes annual snapshot with an inferred new wealth figure. Broader person-specific research remains necessary.

jacqueline-mars.reviewDepth: Source-led review of stated episodes; broader coverage still limited
jacqueline-mars.period: Estate-tax campaign in the 1990s–2000s; report published April 2006
jacqueline-mars.summary: Historical estate-tax research implicates family-company advocacy, but does not establish Jacqueline’s individual direction or return.

john-mars.reviewDepth: Source-led review of stated episodes; broader coverage still limited
john-mars.period: Estate-tax campaign in the 1990s–2000s; report published April 2006
john-mars.summary: John’s family-company political activity is documented; his personal decisions and resulting gains remain unresolved.
john-mars.mechanism: Family-company estate-tax lobbying; person-level control and realized return unresolved

support.text: The report identifies John among the siblings with senior corporate roles and describes payments by Mars Inc. to an estate-tax lobbying group. It does not itemize his personal instructions.
support.source: Public Citizen / United for a Fair Economy, report p. 36

counter.text: Company payments are not automatically John’s personal payments. The report’s estimated family benefit is contingent on repeal, not a demonstrated individual windfall.

john-mars.limitations: No numerical estimate. Family-level research is retained as evidence to investigate, not transferred wholesale to John. More direct evidence of his decisions and policy outcomes is required; lack of a score is not a clean bill of health.

giovanni-ferrero.reviewDepth: Source-led review of stated episodes; broader coverage still limited
giovanni-ferrero.period: European lobbying declarations through 2026; governance announcement, March 2026
giovanni-ferrero.summary: Ferrero International’s policy access is visible in a lobbying-record compilation. Giovanni’s strategic leadership is separately documented, but those facts do not establish that he attended the meetings or obtained a personal preferential decision.

support.text: Ferrero’s March 2026 announcement identifies Giovanni as president of its holding company, with new leadership roles reporting to him and a continuing group strategy remit.

support.source: MEP of the Week: Ferrero International record

giovanni-ferrero.limitations: No score: a corporate meeting log does not establish an individual favor or reciprocal bargain. The EU register page did not expose usable record text during this review, so the compilation is explicitly secondary. Private tax arrangements and business leadership alone do not establish oligarchy.

paolo-ardoino.reviewDepth: Source-led review of stated episodes; broader coverage still limited
paolo-ardoino.period: Volcano Energy announcement, June 2023; licensing and headquarters move, January 2025

paolo-ardoino.mechanism: Executive-led investment and jurisdiction choice ↔ public crypto strategy and sector incentives

support.text: Tether’s January 2025 announcement quotes CEO Ardoino explaining its planned relocation after obtaining a digital-asset license and presents the move as aligned with El Salvador’s policy direction.
Tether’s June 2023 announcement quotes then-CTO Ardoino supporting its participation in Volcano Energy. The project’s billion-dollar ambition is not a statement that Tether alone paid that amount.

support.access: Indexed Reuters article passage reviewed; direct retrieval unavailable

paolo-ardoino.limitations: Historical, episode-limited estimate of a policy partnership, not corruption. It does not establish that Ardoino wrote the law, personally received all company benefits, or paid for a license. Investment announcements are not completed-spending audits. lakshmi-mittal.reviewDepth: Primary-source-led episode review (wave 37); not independently editorially reviewed; not exoneration
lakshmi-mittal.period: Sidex privatization and Blair letter, July–November 2001; Commons scrutiny February–March 2002; contrast episodes 2005 (Ukraine), 2013 (India), 2023 (Kazakhstan)
lakshmi-mittal.summary: Forbes lists Lakshmi Mittal under India, but his business is global, so each episode has its own jurisdiction. The scored episode is UK/Romania, 2001–2002: Tony Blair signed a letter supporting Mittal’s company LNM in Romania’s Sidex privatization while Mittal was a £125,000 Labour donor. The overlap is documented; the government said the donation was unrelated and the award decision preceded the letter, and the Commons rejected the opposition motion. Later episodes point the other way and are not averaged into the score: a live-broadcast 2005 Ukrainian re-auction (Ukraine), an Odisha steel plant abandoned in 2013 over delayed iron-ore blocks (India), and the 2023 Kazakhstan transfer of ArcelorMittal Temirtau to the state after a mine disaster (Kazakhstan). No UK/EU case or Indian coal-block case involving Mittal was found in this review.
lakshmi-mittal.mechanism: Party donation and diplomatic endorsement ↔ disputed influence on a privatization (UK/Romania 2001–02)

support.text: Blair told the Commons it was public record that Mittal was a Labour donor, that the letter he signed mentioned LNM rather than Mittal, and that knowing of the support would have made no difference. The Conservative leader’s question confirms the letter to the Romanian prime minister was signed on 23 July 2001.
support.source: Hansard, 13 February 2002 (Prime Minister’s Questions): Blair and Duncan Smith
support.kind: Parliamentary record: acknowledgment of letter and donor status
support.access: Page text of the Commons sitting read on the historic-Hansard mirror

support.text: The opposition motion (moved by Adam Price) noted the £125,000 Labour donation and Mittal’s non-domiciled status and demanded an inquiry; in debate it was argued that the letter followed within days of the request and that Romania sold Sidex in November after an EBRD loan. These are political arguments, not findings.
support.access: Full debate text read on the historic-Hansard mirror

counter.text: Blair said the letter was written at the British embassy’s request to support Romanian reform and, citing the Romanian prime minister, that the award decision was made before the letter; he refused an inquiry.

Wales Secretary Paul Murphy said the donation had nothing to do with the letter, that the letter was sent after the Sidex decision but before signing, and that the EBRD loan reflected its development mandate. Both the motion (192 to 318) and, on the government amendment, the vote (306 to 181) went the government’s way. A Commons vote is not an adjudication.
counter.access: Full debate text and division counts read

counter.text: In a live-broadcast 2005 auction in Ukraine, Mittal Steel won Kryvorizhstal for about USD 4.8 billion after a court annulled an earlier 2004 sale that had been criticized as corrupt; higher bids in 2004 had been rejected. This is the opposite pattern to patronage, in a different jurisdiction.
counter.source: Wikipedia: Kryvorizhstal (secondary compilation of Kyiv Post and others)
counter.access: Page text read; underlying sources not opened

counter.text: In October 2023 Kazakhstan’s president ordered cooperation with ArcelorMittal to cease after a mine explosion killed 46, and ArcelorMittal signed an agreement to transfer ArcelorMittal Temirtau to the state; RFE/RL says Nazarbayev had enticed Mittal to revive the steelworks, but describes increasingly hostile later official treatment. The company said it would compensate victims and cooperate with the state. This shows state power over the company in Kazakhstan, not a finding on earlier relations.
counter.access: Both articles read; Business Recorder at https://www.brecorder.com/news/amp/40270540

counter.text: ArcelorMittal dropped a planned 12-million-tonne steel plant in Odisha, India, saying delays in land acquisition and allocation of captive iron-ore blocks made it unviable. That is evidence against preferential Indian state benefit in that project, not a general finding.

lakshmi-mittal.limitations: Historical single-episode estimate for UK/Romania 2001–02, not a global or present-day assessment, and not a finding that any contract or letter was purchased. Hansard records assertions, not adjudication; the Romanian procurement file and later ministerial inquiries were not reviewed; the earlier receipts from UK Parliament’s own site were replaced by the identical Commons sittings on the historic-Hansard mirror because the original host blocked automated access. The contrast episodes involve other jurisdictions and are secondary or brief. Rampia/Dipside coal-block, EU merger or antitrust matters and Mittal’s UK donations after 2002 were not reviewed.

rinat-akhmetov.reviewDepth: Source-led historical episode review; not independently editorially reviewed
rinat-akhmetov.period: Kryvorizhstal sale, 2004–2005; ECHR ruling, 2018; media-exit statement, 2022
rinat-akhmetov.summary: Akhmetov’s participation in the politically connected 2004 steel privatization provides a specific historical wealth–power case. The transaction was reversed, but later European human-rights findings against the reversal process prevent treating it as a simple, unqualified vindication of every accusation.

support.text: Reuters identifies Akhmetov and Pinchuk as buyers in the $800 million 2004 sale, subsequently reversed before an open tender fetched approximately $4.8 billion. It identifies Akhmetov as a key Yanukovich backer.

The ECHR’s case-law note describes the acquiring consortium’s owners as linked to the ruling party and presidency. It records the original favorable court decisions, later reopening, return of the purchase money, and resale.
support.source: European Court of Human Rights: Information Note 219, pp. 8–10

counter.text: The ECHR found a fair-hearing violation in the reopening and reversal proceedings, but no property-rights violation, and rejected the pecuniary-damage claim. The findings concern the consortium’s rights, not a criminal conviction of Akhmetov.

In July 2022, Akhmetov announced his group’s exit from media and surrender of licenses in response to the anti-oligarch law, and rejected the oligarch label. The announcement concerns licenses, not transfer of the entire business to the state.

rinat-akhmetov.limitations: The score concerns a historical acquisition, not ongoing possession of the steel mill, a criminal finding, or membership of a current legal register. A later auction’s price is not an exact measure of the earlier discount. The fair-hearing violation and his response are integral to the assessment; present wartime business conditions need separate review.

james-ratcliffe.reviewDepth: Source-led episode review; not independently editorially reviewed
james-ratcliffe.period: Project One support, 2023; policy advocacy and Grangemouth agreement, 2025
james-ratcliffe.summary: Ratcliffe publicly sought policy relief for industry, while INEOS secured named government-backed investments. These are concrete state–business relationships, but the reviewed record also shows public-interest conditions rather than an unrestricted personal windfall.
james-ratcliffe.mechanism: Industrial policy advocacy ↔ government-backed investment with public safeguards

support.text: Reuters reports Ratcliffe personally urging Britain to reduce environmental costs on businesses, presenting high costs as a barrier to investment.

The UK announced more than £120 million of government support within a £150 million joint Grangemouth investment. Its release quotes Ratcliffe welcoming the partnership. These are announced project amounts, not personal payments.
UK Export Finance disclosed €700 million principal support for INEOS Project One and named the participating UK exporters. It is export-finance support, not a €700 million cash gift to Ratcliffe.
support.source: UK Export Finance: supported project notice

counter.text: The Grangemouth announcement identifies jobs and critical supply chains as public objectives. It restricts funding to site improvements, requires an operational commitment, and gives government a right to share future profits.
UKEF required environmental and social performance monitoring. Its notice describes an export-support decision subject to standards, not a finding of political favoritism.

james-ratcliffe.limitations: The estimate concerns documented industrial-policy bargaining, not corruption or a claim that lobbying caused these awards. Announced support is not audited disbursement or profit. The chemicals plant is distinct from the closed oil refinery. Broad industry relief is not exclusive personal privilege.

stephen-ross.reviewDepth: Source-led episode review; not independently editorially reviewed
stephen-ross.period: Hudson Yards reporting, 2017–2019; city elections, 2021; western-yard proposal, 2025
stephen-ross.summary: Ross combined substantial electoral spending with a development business benefiting from public financing and tax incentives. That overlap supports an influence estimate, not a claim that his donations purchased a particular approval.
stephen-ross.mechanism: Private electoral spending ↔ publicly enabled urban development

support.text: The Campaign Finance Board lists Stephen M. Ross as Common Sense NYC’s largest contributor, at $1 million. The committee spent about $1.52 million in City Council races; its total spending is not all Ross’s personal expenditure.
support.source: NYC Campaign Finance Board: 2021 post-election report, p. 93

support.text: Forbes interviews Ross about Hudson Yards and distinguishes an estimated $1.4 billion in tax breaks from $4 billion of other city investment. Those aggregate figures are not a direct payment of the entire sum to him.
support.kind: Reported business benefit and subject interview

support.text: IBO explains that qualifying commercial developments receive discounted payments in lieu of property taxes, whereas residential and hotel developments generally pay full taxes. It separately identifies city infrastructure and interest support.
support.source: NYC Independent Budget Office: Hudson Yards fiscal brief
support.access: Indexed PDF passages reviewed; direct URL now redirects

counter.text: Ross defended the development as connected to the wider city rather than an exclusive enclave. Public infrastructure can benefit others as well as the developer; the full city investment is not his private gain.

The city’s June 2025 western-yard announcement describes a tentative deal including affordable homes, public space and a school, using future project tax revenue for infrastructure. Proposed delivery is not proof of completed public benefits.

stephen-ross.limitations: Historical episode estimate, not proof of vote buying, guaranteed election outcomes or a quid pro quo. The 2021 donations postdate the earlier Hudson Yards arrangements. District-wide costs, tax concessions and company receipts are different quantities. This review does not audit later financing or assign all Related activity to Ross.

idan-ofer.reviewDepth: Source-led episode review; not independently editorially reviewed
idan-ofer.summary: Ofer personally joined high-level lobbying over ICL’s resource-tax exposure. The narrow episode shows political access and investment leverage, but the company’s own subsequent filing confirms that the contested tax legislation passed.

support.text: ICL reported that the Knesset approved legislation implementing Sheshinski II on 18 November 2015 and anticipated an adverse effect on profits, dependent on potash prices.

counter.text: The Prime Minister’s Office characterized the meeting as normal dialogue and said no decisions had been taken; the finance minister supported the reform.
The company’s enactment notice contradicts a claim that the campaign prevented the reform. It does not measure whether lobbying affected any details.

idan-ofer.limitations: The zero benefit level is confined to stopping this reform, not a finding of no concessions or political advantages anywhere in Ofer’s career. The score does not cover later Dead Sea arrangements, whose assets and compensation require separate valuation. Company conduct is attributed to him only where personal involvement is reported.

michal-strnad.reviewDepth: Source-led episode review; not independently editorially reviewed
michal-strnad.period: Slovak framework, December 2025; IPO and company disclosures, 2026
michal-strnad.summary: Strnad’s leadership and CSG’s major government procurement framework are documented. The framework’s headline value is not booked revenue, and the reviewed material does not establish his personal influence over the award or preferential terms.

support.text: The IPO announcement identifies Michal Strnad as owner and chairman, and names him for the chair/CEO role after the proposed corporate conversion.

support.text: CSG’s annual results describe ZVS Holding’s seven-year Slovak Ministry of Defence framework for ammunition for Slovakia and other EU states, with a potential value up to €58 billion.

counter.text: CSG explicitly says €58 billion is a potential framework value, not a committed order book. Individual orders are required, and approximately €1 billion was included in the pipeline at the results announcement. Pipeline is not recognized revenue.

suleiman-kerimov-family.reviewDepth: Source-led episode review; not independently editorially reviewed
suleiman-kerimov-family.period: Uralkali purchase and sale discussions, 2010–2013; Treasury action, 2022

support.text: Treasury identifies Kerimov as a Federation Council member and states that his 2018 designation was for being a Russian government official. Its 2022 notice blocks a trust in which it says he retained an interest.

anthoni-salim-1.reviewDepth: Source-led historical episode review; not independently editorially reviewed
anthoni-salim-1.period: Suharto-era business relationships and post-1998 restructuring; studies published 2007 and 2012
anthoni-salim-1.summary: Research places Anthoni, not only his father, inside the Salim Group’s historical state–business network. It also describes his efforts to reduce dependence on the Suharto relationship. This is a historical assessment, not an assertion of continuing presidential patronage.
anthoni-salim-1.mechanism: Politically connected ventures and industrial-policy service ↔ protection and support

support.text: Dieleman and Boddewyn identify Anthony Salim in management roles in ventures with Suharto-family participants. Their case study also cites his explanation that a steel investment served a government industrialization task.
support.source: Dieleman & Boddewyn: Organization Studies case study, Tables 2–3

support.text: Dieleman’s corporate history describes continuing protected licenses and state support during Anthoni’s modernization efforts, rather than treating every benefit as confined to his father’s founding period.
support.source: Marleen Dieleman: The Rhythm of Strategy, pp. 124–125

counter.text: The same history describes diversification and professional management intended to reduce reliance on political relationships. New politically connected ventures were a minority of the group’s new partnerships.
The manuscript warns that its company-database entries do not necessarily describe still-operating firms or unchanged ownership. Historical board links cannot be presented as current ones.

anthoni-salim-1.limitations: The two works share an author and research base, not two wholly independent investigations. Anthoni is also rendered Anthony in the sources. No personal criminal finding is asserted. Group benefits are linked to his documented management role, not inherited guilt; the extent of his individual direction is less certain than the historical network.

pham-nhat-vuong.reviewDepth: Source-led historical episode review; not independently editorially reviewed
pham-nhat-vuong.summary: Vuong’s newly established railway company sought unusually favorable public financing and received high-level consideration. But the proposal was withdrawn; a request for a subsidy must not be reported as an awarded or paid benefit.
pham-nhat-vuong.mechanism: Owner-founded infrastructure bid → requested public financing, not a completed award

support.text: Reuters links Vuong personally to the newly established VinSpeed and reports a government document welcoming consideration of its bid. The proposal sought state financing for 80% of costs, at zero interest over 35 years.

phil-knight.reviewDepth: Source-led historical episode review; not independently editorially reviewed

phil-knight.limitations: Scoped to these Oregon episodes, not a finding of corruption or an overall account of Nike. Corporate tax treatment is not personal cash income. Knight’s individual direction of the tax negotiations and a reciprocal bargain are not established; the weakest dimension is the link between giving and benefit.

The wide range reflects that uncertainty; nationality and sanctions do not themselves add points.

mikhail-prokhorov.reviewDepth: Source-led historical episode review; not independently editorially reviewed

mikhail-prokhorov.summary: Prokhorov’s role in the bank-led acquisition of Norilsk links his historical wealth formation to a politically structured privatization process. support.text: Szelényi identifies Prokhorov as the bank’s board chairman and describes him working with Potanin to acquire Norilsk Nickel through it. The account also credits his subsequent management and restructuring.

support.kind: Scholarly account of the financing and allocation mechanism
support.access: PDF abstract and printed pages 2 and 8 reviewed directly

support.text: The New Yorker’s interview-based profile identifies both partners as beneficiaries of the Norilsk transaction. Prokhorov describes a division of labor: he favored technical operations, while Potanin handled politics and lobbying.
support.source: Julia Ioffe / The New Yorker: The Master and Mikhail
support.kind: Individual participation and subject’s attribution boundary

counter.text: Treisman challenges the scale of supposed underpricing and later economic damage, despite criticizing execution. His Norilsk discount estimates depend on contemporaneous market valuations; a later company valuation is not the price of the original stake.
counter.source: Daniel Treisman / NBER: valuation and performance qualifications
counter.access: PDF abstract and printed pages 2 and 8 reviewed directly

counter.text: In a Reuters interview during his presidential campaign, Prokhorov denied being a Kremlin instrument and called for democratic reform. These are his stated positions, not independent proof of either political control or independence.
counter.source: Reuters, republished by The Moscow Times
counter.kind: Direct subject response and later political context

mikhail-prokhorov.limitations: Historical editorial assessment, not an allegation of a present-day crime or a comprehensive 2026 political profile. Bank-level participation and personal benefit are documented more clearly than his individual design of the rules. The later campaign is not evidence that the earlier acquisition was an election payment. The score does not treat all privatization, later growth, or Potanin’s conduct as Prokhorov’s misconduct.
